newsitem.title: USA: Firms wary of FASB derivatives proposals.
newsitem.headline: Firms wary of FASB derivatives proposals.

text.p: Company and derivatives industry officials on Monday urged the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) to scuttle proposed changes in accounting rules for derivatives.
The changes would spark volatility in company earnings and spook or mislead investors and analysts, they said on the second day of a four-day hearing on the FASB's proposals.

"The market will react negatively to accounting changes that increase earnings volatility," said Charles Smithson, a member of the board of directors of the International Swap & Derivatives Association.
"I'm positive that the change will be for the worse."

At issue is the FASB's proposal to require companies to carry all derivatives, on their balance sheets at current market values. Under current practice, many derivatives -- financial instruments whose value is based on the value of another instrument, asset or market index -- are carried off-balance sheet, and similar transactions may receive disparate accounting treatment.
The FASB heard overwhelmingly negative feedback on its proposed treatment of changes in the value of derivatives once they are carried on balance sheets.
Michael Conley, the chief financial officer of McDonald's Corp, said the FASB's proposed overhaul had "four fatal flaws."
Among them would be the addition of "artificial volatility to financial statements," said Conley.

He said that, even though McDonald's had no plans to use derivatives for trading purposes, the proposed changes would lead to "bad accounting" because they would "require us to use longer-term hedging instruments."
Representatives of major insurers also expressed fears.

"This proposal for derivatives accounting, however well- intentioned, in many instances fails to adequately represent the underlying economics of very legitimate risk reducing strategies," said David Hall, senior vice president and actuary at ITT Hartford.
"Reducing asset-liability gap risk is a very common derivatives application in the insurance industry," said Hall.

"The most direct solution to these anomalies would be to incorporate effectiveness evaluations which incorporate cash flows from all conponents of the transaction -- namely, the assets, liabilities and hedge," he said.

Bob Reitano, vice president of John Hancock Life Insurance's investment policy and research department, said it was unfortunate that FASB's proposal did not "provide an accounting basis which distinguishes between the hedging and speculative uses of derivatives."
Only one respondent on Monday voiced support for "certain features" of the FASB's proposal.

"We strongly believe that there is a need for a broad and comprehensive standard that would achieve consistent accounting results, regardless of the type of derivative used," said Bob Herz, Coopers & Lybrand's national director of accounting and SEC services.

However, Herz added that it might be "impossible at this time to develop a workable and understandable accounting model for derivatives and hedging transactions that would always achieve both the objective of carrying all derivatives at fair value, while at the same time producing accounting results that faithfully portray the intent and effect of many transactions involving derivatives."
